```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", fig.width = 8, fig.height = 5, dpi = 90)
has <- requireNamespace("ss3diags", quietly = TRUE) && requireNamespace("mvtnorm", quietly = TRUE) &&
  requireNamespace("MASS", quietly = TRUE)
library(ss3diags2)
```

`ss3diags2` extracts observations and outputs of Stock Synthesis (SS3) models, read with `r4ss::SS_output()`, into
long `data.table` tables that convert to FLR objects (`FLQuants`, `FLIndices`, `FLStockR`, `FLPar`), and plots them
with `ggplot2`. Inputs are shaped for JABBA3 and FLicc. This guide walks through the workflow and flags points that
matter for advice. The examples use `ss3ank` (black anglerfish, in the package) and the `ss3diags` example models.

# 1. Observations

```{r obs}
data(ss3ank)
ss3_fleets(ss3ank)
lfd <- ss3_lencomp(ss3ank)          # FLQuants by fleet (and partition), sex as unit
idx <- ss3_indices(ss3ank)          # FLIndices of FLIndexBiomass, input SE in index.var
ss3plot_data(catch = ss3_catch(ss3ank), indices = idx, lencomp = lfd, by = "unit")
```

`ss2jabba3()` and `ss2flicc()` return the same observations shaped as JABBA3 and FLicc inputs (catch in weight by
fleet, annual indices with input SEs; length compositions by gear on common bins and years).

# 2. Composition residuals

One-step-ahead (OSA) residuals follow the SS3 likelihood (multinomial, or Dirichlet-multinomial with the precision
implied by the SS3 effective sample size). Cohort tracks of von Bertalanffy growth by sex help to see year classes.

```{r osa, fig.height = 7}
r <- ss3_resid(ss3ank)
ss3plot_resid(r, lhpar = ss3_lhpar(ss3ank))
```

OSA residuals are conditional on the smaller bins: too few small fish gives negative residuals at small lengths
and positive residuals at larger lengths.

# 3. Stock status: FLStockR and MVLN

`ss3stk()` builds the simplified `FLStockR` of `FLRef::ss2FLStockR()`: maximum likelihood estimates with standard
errors (`output = "mle"`), or draws from a multivariate lognormal (MVLN) approximation (`output = "iters"`,
`ss3mvln()`).

* `ss3mvln(method = "joint")` (default) draws SSB, recruitment and F of all years and the reference points from one
  MVLN with the full correlation matrix of the SS3 derived quantities (Kell et al. 2023; the `ss3om::ssmvln()`
  approach). Each iteration is a coherent trajectory and the reference points have iterations.
* `ss3mvln(method = "annual")` is the delta-MVLN of `ss3diags::SSdeltaMVLN()` (Walter and Winker 2020;
  Winker et al. 2019), drawn year by year.

```{r mvln, eval = has}
data(natl.sma, package = "ss3diags")
stk <- ss3stk(ss3sma, output = "iters", iters = 500, fwd = TRUE)
ss3plot_trj(stk, type = c("B/Btgt", "F/Ftgt", "Catch"), ncol = 1)
```

**Note on SSdeltaMVLN.** For the example models the year-by-year delta-MVLN understates the correlation between
B/Bmsy and F/Fmsy in the terminal year (shortfin mako: -0.24, against -0.86 in the SS3 covariance; Pacific hake:
-0.26 against -0.76), so its Kobe clouds are rounder than the estimated uncertainty. The joint method keeps the
estimated correlation. Use `method = "joint"` for advice.

# 4. Kobe plots and the timing of F and SSB  {#kobe-lag}

> **Critical for advice.** SS3 reports SSB at spawning (typically at the start of the year), and F of year *y* acts
> during year *y*. The SSB that results from the fishing in year *y* is therefore SSB in year *y + 1*. The usual Kobe
> plot pairs F(*y*) with SSB(*y*): it shows the biomass the fishery in *y* started from, not the biomass it led to.
> When F is well above Fmsy, the stock status that follows from the current exploitation can be markedly worse
> than the plot of F(*y*) against SSB(*y*) suggests. Advice should state which convention is used and, when the
> two differ, show both.

`ss3plot_kobe(lag = 1)` plots F(*y*) against B/Btgt(*y + 1*). The uncertainty cloud then pairs F(*Y*) with B(*Y + 1*)
within each iteration, which needs draws linked across years: use `ss3mvln(method = "joint")` (a warning is given for
year-by-year draws). Build the stock with `fwd = TRUE` so that SSB at the start of the year after the last assessment
year (reported by SS3 as a forecast quantity) is available; F is used up to the end year only.

```{r kobe, eval = has, fig.width = 11, fig.height = 4.5}
k0 <- ss3plot_kobe(stk) + ggplot2::ggtitle("lag = 0: F(y) against B(y)")
k1 <- ss3plot_kobe(stk, lag = 1) + ggplot2::ggtitle("lag = 1: F(y) against B(y + 1)")
if(requireNamespace("patchwork", quietly = TRUE)) patchwork::wrap_plots(k0, k1) else k1
```

For North Atlantic shortfin mako the probability of being overfished and subject to overfishing (red quadrant) in
2015 is about 78% with F(2015) against SSB(2015) and about 93% with F(2015) against SSB(2016).

Points to check before using the lagged plot for advice:

* SSB(*y + 1*) for the last assessment year is a one-year forecast: it depends on the SS3 forecast settings
  (`forecast.ss`) and, where recruits mature within a year, on the forecast recruitment.
* Kell et al. (2023) pair F and SSB both ways in their figures (F in 2020 with SSB in 2021, and both in 2022); the
  convention is not standardised, which is why it must be stated with the advice.

# 5. Production function and equilibrium

`ss3_spm()` fits a Pella-Tomlinson production function to the SS3 equilibrium yield curve and checks it against
the SS3 benchmarks. SS3 holds several "unfished" states: SSB_Virgin (start-year biology), SSB_unfished (benchmark
years) and the dynamic B0 of each year; with time-varying weight-at-age or M (empirical `wtatage`) these differ, and
the equilibrium table can rest on yet another biology. `ss3_spm()` warns when its fit and the SS3 benchmarks differ.

# 6. Season-, sex- and area-structured models: fleets, partial F and impact

The northern shrimp assessment (`data(ss3pra)`) has four seasons, two sexes (hermaphrodite) and two areas with
area-specific fleets. The extraction functions keep this structure in the FLQuant dimensions (unit = sex, season,
area), so the observation plots split by any of them, e.g. `ss3plot_catch(ss3_catch(ss3pra), by = c("season", "area"))`.

```{r pra, eval = FALSE}
data(ss3pra)
fa <- ss3_fa(ss3pra)                    # F-at-age by fleet: age, year, unit, season, area
ss3plot_fa(fa)
pf <- ss3_partialF(ss3pra, groups = list(Denmark = 1:2, Norway = 3:4, Sweden = 5:6))
ss3plot_partialF(pf)                    # partial F's add up to the reported Fbar
ss3plot_partialF(ss3_partialF(ss3pra, groups = "area", method = "fbar"))   # F by area
imp <- ss3_impact(ss3pra, groups = list(Denmark = 1:2, Norway = 3:4, Sweden = 5:6))
imp$check                               # projected vs SS3 SSB and dynamic B0
ss3plot_impact(imp)
```

Two notions of F by area should not be confused. The partial F from `method = "catch"` is each fleet's (or area's)
share of the stock F and adds up to the reported F. The F from `method = "fbar"` is the mortality experienced by the
fish in the area where a fleet operates; F's of fleets in the same area add up, but F's of different areas do not add
up to the stock F when the stock is spread over the areas.

`ss3_impact()` follows Wang et al. (2009): SSB is projected without fishing and with the fleet groups added one by
one, so the impact of each group is the SSB it removes, and all impacts add up to dynamic B0 minus SSB. It runs on
the SS3 report, with the realised SS3 mortality, spawning output and recruitment deviations, and its no-fishing
projection reproduces the SS3 dynamic B0. The order in which groups are added matters for the share of each group
when the stock-recruit relationship is not flat.

North Atlantic blue shark. Collect. Vol. Sci. Pap. ICCAT, 80(4): 837-858 (SCRS/2023/143).

Trijoulet, V., Albertsen, C.M., Kristensen, K., Legault, C.M., Miller, T.J. and Nielsen, A. (2023). Model validation
